markets.author: Kedma Hamelberg
markets.title: The choices around AI are becoming more visible
markets.deck: This week’s stories were less about one big technical leap and more about the choices that shape everyday use.
markets.summary: This week’s stories were less about one big technical leap and more about the choices that shape everyday use. AWS introduced a tool to help coding agents prepare AI systems for deployment, while a French analysis linked AI-exposed jobs with early changes in youth hiring. Neither story proves a wider outcome on its own. Elsewhere, an international forum called for shared rules and cooperation, Greenpeace France focused on environmental and social costs, and Spain’s new HR rules emphasised transparency and meaningful human oversight. Taken together, these are five separate reports, not a single global trend. But they point to the same question: can useful AI systems be built with care for work, power, resources and accountability?

research.author: Kedma Hamelberg
research.title: Remembering more is not always enough
research.deck: Two studies this week look at how AI systems use the past to act in the present.
research.summary: Two studies this week look at how AI systems use the past to act in the present. One tested Ledger, a memory tool that records where objects are and how they move in first-person video. It answered some later spatial questions without replaying the video, but became less reliable when the scene changed. The second study found that longer video history helped a robot control task only when the model had first learned to predict what might happen next. More stored information alone was not the answer. Both papers suggest that useful AI memory depends on how information is organised and trained, not simply on how much of it is kept.
